comments.author: viewer-026523fa4a
comments.text: The $2,000 question works because price is a commitment device that operates on both sides of the transaction. On the buyer side, it is the sunk cost effect running in your favour for once: Arkes and Blumer (1985) found that the more people pay, the more compelled they feel to show up and extract the value — which is why a $200 course gets bought and never watched, while a $2,000 cohort gets finished. On the seller side, the high price removes your hiding place. At $200, a student who quietly disappears is their problem. At $2,000, you have taken on an obligation you can actually feel, so you build the feedback loops and hire the help. The sharpest part is that the price did not just signal quality. It manufactured it, by changing what both parties did next.

comments.text: The game framing works because games make progress legible. Amabile and Kramer's progress principle (2011) found that of everything shaping a workday, the strongest driver of motivation and mood is the sense of making progress in meaningful work — and games are machines for manufacturing exactly that signal: a score, a level, feedback within seconds. A revenue dashboard does the same thing for the keystrokes that feel like drudgery inside a job, where progress can stay invisible for months. The catch is the other mechanic hiding in the examples: survivorship. We hear from the ten people whose key presses became Instagram because they won. The thousands who pressed keys in much the same order and got a quiet shutdown instead never get quoted — the game is real, but the leaderboard only ever shows the winners.

comments.text:
Ali, I found a way to have Claude edit my videos. What used to take me ~6 hours now takes ~40 minutes of Claude's time (plus my final check). My workflow, if useful:

1. One folder per video with the raw footage. I export the audio, clean the echo with Adobe Podcast Enhance, sync it in Final Cut and export the project as XML.
2. I give Claude the full script and ask where a visual or B-roll would help. We agree on the list, it generates the animations plus a "readme" saying exactly where each one goes.
3. Music and SFX in an "audio" subfolder, the hook made with HyperFrames in a "hook" subfolder.
4. Claude Code works in the folder: removes retakes, pauses over 0.2s and background noise, places the animations from the readme, adds the hook, and writes a new XML.
5. I import it into Final Cut, check, polish, export in 4K.

The trick: a word-for-word script. Claude compares the footage with it, so it knows which take to keep.

What I don't delegate: the idea, the script, the final call on visuals. Thanks for the inspiration!

comments.author: viewer-026523fa4a
comments.text: The comparison hiding inside this comparison is how the edits get judged once you know who — or what — made them. Dietvorst, Simmons and Massey (2015) documented algorithm aversion: after seeing an algorithm make one visible mistake, people abandon it far more readily than a human who errs the same way, even when the algorithm is better on average. That maps uncomfortably well onto the 'What Went Wrong' round — an AI error reads as proof the whole approach is broken, while a human editor's rough edges read as fixable drafts. Layer on the effort heuristic (Kruger et al., 2004): people rate work as higher quality when they believe more time and effort went into it. A professional editor's hours are visible in the invoice; a model's minutes are invisible, so identical polish gets discounted. The blind version of this test — same two edits, no labels, no times attached — would be the real verdict, because right now the judging is running on authorship as much as on frames.

comments.videoTitle: Overthinking your niche? Do this
comments.author: viewer-026523fa4a
comments.text: This is the exploration versus exploitation problem in disguise. Planning a niche forever is pure exploration with no feedback, so you never learn what actually resonates. Posting first flips it: action generates data, and the audience's response — not your initial guess — defines the niche. It is the same reason analysis paralysis feels productive while producing nothing: thinking about the choice substitutes for testing it.
